questions.question_text: Which international organization publishes the annual Human Development Report comparing countries based on health, education, and income?
options: Option C) United Nations Development Programme (UNDP)
questions.correct_answer: Option C) United Nations Development Programme (UNDP)

questions.question_text: What is the formula used to calculate the Per Capita Income of a country?
options: Option A) Total National Income / Total Population
Option B) Total Exports / Total Imports
Option C) Gross Domestic Product / Working Population
Option D) Total Revenue / Total Land Area
questions.correct_answer: Option A) Total National Income / Total Population

questions.question_text: According to the World Bank Development Report (2021), countries with a per capita income above which threshold are classified as high-income countries?
Explain why Per Capita Income alone is considered an inadequate metric for comparing national development across countries.
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Per Capita Income is an average that hides income distribution disparities (wealth concentration among elites).
2. It ignores non-material indicators such as literacy rate, life expectancy, and infant mortality rate.
3. It excludes social factors like freedom, security, gender equality, and environmental health.

questions.question_text: Define Infant Mortality Rate (IMR) and Net Attendance Ratio.
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
Infant Mortality Rate (IMR): The number of children that die before completing one year of age as a proportion of 1,000 live children born in that specific year.
Net Attendance Ratio: The total number of children of age group 14 and 15 years attending school as a percentage of total number of children in the same age group.

questions.question_text: Compare Haryana, Kerala, and Bihar in terms of Per Capita Income and human development indicators. Explain why Kerala ranks higher overall despite having lower average income than Haryana.
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Economic Data: Haryana has a higher per capita income (₹2,36,147) than Kerala (₹2,21,904) and Bihar (₹40,982).
2. Health & Education Indicators: Kerala surpasses Haryana with a lower Infant Mortality Rate (7 vs 30 per 1,000), higher Literacy Rate (94% vs 80%), and higher Net Attendance Ratio (83% vs 61%).
3. Explanation: Monetary wealth cannot buy essential public goods. Kerala invested systematically in state-funded primary healthcare, public distribution systems (PDS), and universal primary education, making it more humanly developed.

questions.question_text:
Read the text and answer: 'Groundwater is a renewable resource, but over-exploitation in agricultural regions of Punjab and Western UP has led to severe water table depletion. Over one-third of Indian districts report critical groundwater loss.'
(i) Why is groundwater classified as a renewable resource? (1 mark)
(ii) How does over-pumping threaten sustainable development? (1 mark)
(iii) Suggest two policy measures to conserve groundwater resources. (2 marks)
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
(i) Groundwater is naturally replenished by rainfall percolation through soil.
(ii) When extraction rates exceed natural rainfall recharge, water tables collapse, turning a renewable resource into a depleted one and endangering future agricultural production.
(iii) Measures: 1. Promote micro-irrigation (drip and sprinkler systems); 2. Enact rainwater harvesting mandates and regulate tube-well depth.

questions.question_text: Which metric is primarily used by the World Bank in its World Development Reports to categorize nations?
In India, the Literacy Rate measures the proportion of literate population in which age group?
What was India's Per Capita Income classification in 2021 according to World Bank criteria?
Explain why different people have different and sometimes conflicting developmental goals. Provide a suitable example.
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Different people have distinct socio-economic backgrounds, occupations, and immediate life needs.
2. Conflicting Goals: Progress for one group can be destructive for another. Example: Industrialists desiring large hydroelectric dams for electricity vs. indigenous tribal communities whose land and livelihoods are submerged by dam construction.

questions.question_text: Why does money in one's pocket fail to buy all the goods and services required for a quality life?
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Money cannot protect individuals from infectious diseases unless community health infrastructure exists.
2. It cannot buy an unpolluted environment, clean air, or peaceful society.
3. It cannot guarantee freedom from discrimination or guarantee collective security.

questions.question_text: Explain the concept of Sustainable Development. Discuss Mahatma Gandhi's statement: 'The Earth has enough resources to meet the needs of all, but not enough to satisfy the greed of even one person.'
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Concept: Sustainable development meets present societal needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs.
2. Gandhi's Quote Analysis: Emphasizes resource conservation over reckless exploitation. Natural assets (minerals, fossil fuels, groundwater) are finite.
3. Over-exploitation driven by commercial greed depletes stocks rapidly, causing environmental degradation, climate disruption, and inter-generational inequality.
4. Sustainable growth requires equitable distribution, renewable energy adoption, and ecological conservation policies.

questions.question_text:
Read the case scenario: 'A major real estate company acquires agricultural land near an urban metropolis to construct luxury high-rise apartments. While property investors foresee high financial returns, local tenant farmers face eviction without compensation.'
(i) Identify the two contrasting developmental goals in this scenario. (1 mark)
(ii) Why is this scenario an example of conflicting development? (1 mark)
(iii) What measures should the local government adopt to balance progress with social justice? (2 marks)
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
(i) Real estate investors seek capital expansion and profit; tenant farmers seek land security, agricultural livelihood, and shelter.
(ii) Progress for real estate investors directly causes economic displacement and loss of income for tenant farmers.
(iii) Government should enforce rehabilitation policies, provide fair compensation, and guarantee alternative livelihood training for evicted families.

questions.question_text: What is the formula used to determine Body Mass Index (BMI) for evaluating adult nutritional status?
Which Indian state has recorded the lowest Infant Mortality Rate of 7 per 1,000 live births?
An adult individual having a Body Mass Index (BMI) below 18.5 is categorized as:
Distinguish between material goals and non-material goals in human development.
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
Material Goals: Tangible economic assets and income (higher wages, land ownership, cars, housing).
Non-Material Goals: Intangible human entitlements essential for dignity (equal treatment, personal freedom, physical security, respect, non-discrimination, work-life balance).

questions.question_text: Explain the role of the Public Distribution System (PDS) in supporting human development indicators.
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. PDS provides subsidized essential food grains (wheat, rice) to low-income households.
2. It prevents malnutrition, reduces infant mortality, and improves average Body Mass Index (BMI).
3. States with well-functioning PDS (e.g. Tamil Nadu) show significantly better population health than states with weak PDS.

questions.question_text: Describe the key dimensions evaluated in the UNDP Human Development Index (HDI). Contrast HDI with the World Bank's Per Capita Income criterion.
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. UNDP HDI Dimensions:
   - Health: Life expectancy at birth.
   - Education: Mean years of schooling and expected years of schooling.
   - Standard of Living: Gross National Income (GNI) per capita (PPP USD).
2. Contrast with World Bank:
   - World Bank uses a single economic metric (Per Capita Income), ignoring healthcare access, educational quality, and wealth distribution.
   - UNDP HDI provides a holistic, multi-dimensional assessment of human capability and well-being.

questions.question_text:
Read the excerpt: 'Global crude oil reserves are estimated at 1,691 billion barrels, sufficient to last roughly 50 years at current global consumption rates. Developed nations consume crude oil at five times the rate of developing countries.'
(i) Why is crude oil classified as an exhaustible natural resource? (1 mark)
(ii) Identify the international inequity highlighted in crude oil consumption. (1 mark)
(iii) Suggest two long-term strategies for nations to sustain economic activity as crude oil reserves decline. (2 marks)
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
(i) Crude oil has a fixed geological stock that takes millions of years to form and cannot be replenished within human timescales.
(ii) Developed nations consume disproportionately higher oil per capita compared to developing nations.
(iii) Strategies: 1. Accelerate investment in renewable energy (solar, wind, green hydrogen); 2. Expand electrified mass public transportation systems.

questions.question_text: Which non-material factor is crucial for encouraging higher female labor force participation?
options: Option B) Safe and secure environment with shared domestic responsibilities
questions.correct_answer: Option B) Safe and secure environment with shared domestic responsibilities

questions.question_text: Life Expectancy at Birth measures which aspect of national development?
options: Option B) Health and longevity of citizens
Option C) Per capita economic wealth
questions.correct_answer: Option B) Health and longevity of citizens

questions.question_text: Which of the following is an example of an exhaustible natural resource?
How is Body Mass Index (BMI) used to evaluate nutritional status? Calculate the BMI of an individual weighing 50 kg with a height of 1.6 meters.
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Usage: BMI evaluates adult body mass relative to height to detect undernourishment (<18.5) or overweight status (>=25).
2. Calculation: BMI = Weight / (Height)² = 50 / (1.6 × 1.6) = 50 / 2.56 = 19.53 kg/m² (Normal weight range).

questions.question_text: What is meant by National Development? How should a government decide between competing national development priorities?
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Definition: National development refers to a country's capacity to enhance citizen living standards, health, education, infrastructure, and economic equity.
2. Decision Principle: Governments must prioritize fair and just paths that benefit the majority of citizens rather than a small privileged elite, balancing short-term economic growth with ecological sustainability.

questions.question_text: 'Public facilities are essential because individual income alone cannot purchase all the goods and services required for a healthy and dignified life.' Analyze this statement with four supporting arguments.
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Health Security: Money cannot protect individuals from community epidemics or pollution without state public health and sanitation systems.
2. Education Access: Private schooling is unaffordable for poor families; state-funded public schools ensure universal literacy and school attendance.
3. Food Security: Public Distribution System (PDS) ensures low-income families get subsidized food grains, preventing malnutrition.
4. Cost Efficiency: Collective provision of public services (e.g. security, transport, street lighting) is far cheaper and more equitable than individual private arrangements.

questions.question_text:
Examine the hypothetical data:
- Country A: 5 citizens earning ₹9,500, ₹10,000, ₹10,500, ₹10,000, ₹10,000. (Average: ₹10,000)
- Country B: 5 citizens earning ₹500, ₹500, ₹500, ₹500, ₹48,000. (Average: ₹10,000)
(i) Calculate the per capita income for both countries. (1 mark)
(ii) In which country would a citizen of average means prefer to live and why? (1 mark)
(iii) What major limitation of average income does this comparison demonstrate? (2 marks)
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
(i) Per Capita Income is ₹10,000 for both Country A and Country B.
(ii) Country A, because wealth is equitably distributed among citizens without extreme poverty.
(iii) Average income hides income distribution; it fails to show whether wealth is shared among all citizens or concentrated in the hands of a single rich individual.

questions.question_text: The proportion of literate population in the 7 and above age group is known as:
Infant Mortality Rate (IMR) indicates the number of children dying before completing 1 year per how many live births?
What is likely to be a primary developmental goal for an urban unemployed youth?
options: Option A) Higher support prices for crops
Option B) Permanent employment with decent wages
Option D) Construction of village canals
questions.correct_answer: Option B) Permanent employment with decent wages

questions.question_text: Why is groundwater considered a renewable natural resource? Under what conditions does it become endangered?
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Renewable Status: Groundwater is continuously recharged by nature through rainwater seepage into underlying rock aquifers.
2. Endangered Status: It becomes endangered when extraction via deep tube-wells exceeds natural annual rainfall recharge, causing water tables to collapse permanently.

questions.question_text: Explain how equal treatment and freedom act as key non-monetary developmental aspirations.
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Dignity and Freedom: Human beings value self-respect, personal autonomy, and freedom of expression as much as financial earnings.
2. Non-Discrimination: Discrimination based on caste, gender, or religion stifles personal growth; equal treatment ensures equitable access to social and economic opportunities.

questions.question_text: Examine the socio-economic factors that explain why Kerala has superior health and educational achievements compared to Haryana, despite Haryana's higher average per capita income.
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Historical Investment: Kerala made long-term investments in public health centers, mother-child care, and universal primary education.
2. Efficient PDS: Kerala maintains an effective Public Distribution System ensuring food security and nutrition across rural communities.
3. Female Literacy: High female literacy in Kerala directly correlates with lower infant mortality and higher health awareness.
4. Social Infrastructure Priority: Haryana prioritized commercial and agrarian income generation without matching investments in public healthcare and educational infrastructure.

questions.question_text:
Read the passage: 'When women engage in paid employment, their social status and domestic dignity increase. However, if women face unsafe working environments or harassment, their participation declines. Shared domestic work and safe transportation encourage female labor force participation.'
(i) State one non-material benefit women gain from paid employment. (1 mark)
(ii) What prerequisite conditions are necessary to expand female employment? (1 mark)
(iii) Explain how gender equality in employment contributes to broader national development. (2 marks)
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
(i) Enhanced domestic dignity, household decision-making power, and social respect.
(ii) Safe and secure working environments, protection against harassment, and shared domestic responsibilities within families.
(iii) Utilizing female labor expands national economic output, improves child health/education, and fosters an equitable, inclusive society.

questions.question_text: Which economic sector includes activities that extract or harvest natural resources directly, such as agriculture, fishing, forestry, and mining?
What statutory act legally guarantees 100 days of wage employment per year to rural households in India?
options: Option B) Right to Information Act

questions.question_text: To prevent double counting when calculating Gross Domestic Product (GDP), which items are included?
options: Option B) Only final goods and services
Option C) Raw materials and intermediate goods
Option D) Total agricultural produce only
questions.correct_answer: Option B) Only final goods and services

questions.question_text: Distinguish between Primary, Secondary, and Tertiary sectors of the economy with one example of each.
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Primary Sector: Direct exploitation of natural resources (e.g. Cotton cultivation, Mining).
2. Secondary Sector: Manufacturing/processing raw materials into industrial goods (e.g. Spinning cotton into yarn, Manufacturing steel).
3. Tertiary Sector: Support services facilitating production and trade (e.g. Transporting yarn, Banking, IT services).

questions.question_text: Explain what is meant by Disguised Unemployment (Underemployment) in the agricultural sector.
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Definition: A situation where more people work on a farm than are actually required.
2. Feature: Individual marginal labor productivity is zero; removing excess family members does not reduce total crop output.
3. Context: Prevalent among smallholder rural families lacking alternative off-farm employment.

questions.question_text: Compare the Organised sector with the Unorganised sector across employment security, adherence to government rules, working hours, and social security benefits.
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Organised Sector:
   - Registered with government, follows statutory laws (Minimum Wages Act, Factories Act).
   - Formal appointment letter, guaranteed job security, fixed working hours with paid overtime.
   - Mandatory provident fund, medical benefits, and paid holidays.
2. Unorganised Sector:
   - Small unregistered units operating outside legal control.
   - Insecure employment (dismissal anytime), long unregulated hours without overtime pay.
   - Low wages, no paid leave, no medical safety or retirement pensions.

questions.question_text:
Read the case study: 'Laxmi owns 2 hectares of unirrigated land dependent on rain. All five members of her family work on the plot year-round. A local landlord hires two family members to work on his irrigation canal project, paying them daily wages.'
(i) What type of unemployment did Laxmi's family face initially? (1 mark)
(ii) Why did farm yield remain unchanged after two members left to work on the canal? (1 mark)
(iii) Explain how state irrigation investments help eliminate underemployment in rural areas. (2 marks)
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
(i) Disguised Unemployment (Underemployment).
(ii) Because five workers were doing work that three could manage easily; the marginal productivity of the extra two workers was zero.
(iii) Constructing canals/wells enables multi-cropping (farming two or three crops annually), keeping farm family members gainfully employed throughout the year.

questions.question_text: Which economic sector transforms raw sugarcane into sugar and gur?
Underemployment occurs when workers are:
options: Option A) Working less than their potential and capability
Option B) Refusing to work due to low wages
Option C) Employed in MNC corporate offices
questions.correct_answer: Option A) Working less than their potential and capability

questions.question_text: Public sector enterprises are primarily motivated by which objective?
options: Option A) Maximizing private shareholder profit
Option B) Social welfare and public service
questions.correct_answer: Option B) Social welfare and public service

questions.question_text: Why are intermediate goods excluded when calculating Gross Domestic Product (GDP)? Give an example.
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Reason: The value of intermediate goods is already included in the final price of the finished product. Counting them separately leads to double counting.
2. Example: A baker buys wheat flour for ₹10 and sugar for ₹5 to bake a biscuit packet sold for ₹25. Including ₹10 flour and ₹5 sugar along with ₹25 biscuit would artificially inflate GDP.

questions.question_text: Suggest three practical measures to generate additional employment opportunities in rural India.
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Infrastructure Investment: Construct dams, irrigation canals, and rural connectivity roads.
2. Credit Access: Provide low-interest bank loans for small farmers to buy seeds, pumpsets, and fertilizers.
3. Agro-Processing: Establish local dal mills, cold storage units, and honey collection centers in rural clusters.

questions.question_text: Analyze the historical shift in sectoral share of GDP versus employment in India from 1973-74 to 2013-14. Why did employment not shift out of agriculture proportionally?
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Sectoral GDP Shift: Tertiary sector GDP share expanded dramatically to over 50%, while Secondary sector grew moderately, and Primary sector share dropped.
2. Employment Lag: Primary sector still employs >44% of labor force while contributing under 16% to GDP.
3. Reasons for Lag:
   - Secondary sector industrial output grew 9 times, but employment grew only 3 times.
   - Tertiary sector output grew 14 times, but employment grew only 5 times.
   - Service growth was capital-intensive and skill-heavy (IT, banking), failing to absorb unskilled rural agricultural labor.

questions.question_text:
Examine the profiles:
- Kanta: Works in a government office, receives a formal appointment letter, monthly salary on 1st, provident fund, medical allowances, and paid Sundays.
- Kamal: Works in a local grocery shop, gets no appointment letter, works 12 hours daily, receives low daily wages without paid holidays or medical safety.
(i) Classify Kanta and Kamal into economic employment sectors. (1 mark)
(ii) State two social security benefits Kanta enjoys that Kamal lacks. (1 mark)
(iii) Why do informal workers like Kamal need government statutory protection? (2 marks)
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
(i) Kanta works in the Organised Sector; Kamal works in the Unorganised Sector.
(ii) Provident fund (PF) and paid sick leave / medical allowances.
(iii) Informal workers face low irregular wages, arbitrary dismissal, and dangerous work conditions without legal defense unless protected by government labor regulations.

questions.question_text: Activities that assist in the transport, storage, banking, and marketing of industrial goods belong to which sector?
What percentage of India's labor force remains employed in the Primary (Agricultural) sector?
If MGNREGA 2005 fails to assign employment to an eligible applicant within 15 days, what statutory provision applies?
options: Option A) The applicant receives free land
Option B) The state pays a statutory daily unemployment allowance
Option C) The applicant is imprisoned
Option D) No compensation is paid
questions.correct_answer: Option B) The state pays a statutory daily unemployment allowance

questions.question_text: Explain sectoral interdependence using the production chain connecting cotton farming, textile mills, and garment retail.
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Primary to Secondary: Cotton farming (Primary) supplies raw cotton fiber to textile factories (Secondary).
2. Secondary to Tertiary: Textile mills convert fiber into fabric, which requires transport, banking, and insurance (Tertiary) to reach retail markets.
3. Interdependence Impact: A strike by truck drivers or a rise in cotton prices affects factory production and retail clothing sales simultaneously.

questions.question_text: Why does the unorganised sector require active government protection and intervention?
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Vulnerable Workers: Comprises casual construction labor, street vendors, and landless agricultural laborers who lack bargaining power.
2. Exploitative Conditions: Subject to sub-minimum wages, excessive working hours, and lack of safety equipment.
3. Social Insecurity: Zero medical cover or old-age pensions leave families destitute during illness or job loss.

questions.question_text: 'The Public Sector plays a critical role in national development that the Private Sector cannot replace.' Evaluate this statement with five key arguments.
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Heavy Capital Investment: Projects like railways, dams, highways, and power grids require huge investments with long gestation periods that private firms avoid.
2. Affordable Public Utilities: Public sector provides electricity, water, and public transport at subsidized rates to ensure universal access.
3. Support for Poor Citizens: Operates Public Distribution System (PDS) to buy grain from farmers at MSP and supply food to poor households.
4. Balanced Regional Growth: Sets up public plants in backward areas to generate employment and reduce regional economic inequality.
5. Social Infrastructure: State funding builds public health centers and schools essential for human capital development.

questions.question_text:
Read the scenario: 'Truck drivers transport raw sugarcane from rural farms to sugar mills in neighboring industrial towns. Due to a strike by transport unions, trucks remain parked for a week, causing harvested sugarcane to rot in fields and forcing sugar factories to shutdown.'
(i) Which sector does truck transport belong to? (1 mark)
(ii) How does this scenario prove sectoral interdependence? (1 mark)
(iii) Suggest two risk mitigation measures for sugarcane farmers facing transport disruptions. (2 marks)
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
(i) Tertiary (Services) Sector.
(ii) Disruption in Tertiary transport directly paralyzed Primary agricultural sales and Secondary factory production.
(iii) Measures: 1. Establish localized cooperative processing units closer to farms; 2. Implement contractual multi-modal transport agreements.

questions.question_text: Which of the following activities belongs to the Tertiary sector?
options: Option B) Weaving cloth on a handloom
Option C) Call center customer support
questions.correct_answer: Option C) Call center customer support

questions.question_text: TATA Motors and Reliance Industries are examples of enterprises in which sector?
The statutory unemployment allowance under MGNREGA 2005 is triggered if work is not assigned within how many days?
Explain how public expenditure on rural dams, canals, and cold storage creates off-farm employment.
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Direct Construction Jobs: Building dams and canals generates immediate manual employment for rural laborers.
2. Agricultural Multi-Cropping: Canal irrigation allows farmers to grow two or three crops annually, increasing farm labor demand.
3. Storage & Marketing: Cold storage units create jobs in sorting, packaging, transport, and commercial trading.

questions.question_text: Distinguish between Open Unemployment and Disguised Unemployment.
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
Open Unemployment: A worker who is actively seeking work is visibly without any job and earns zero income.
Disguised Unemployment: A worker appears employed on a farm or shop, but their presence is redundant; removing them leaves total output unchanged.

questions.question_text: Analyze the reasons for the dramatic growth of the Tertiary (Service) sector in India, explaining why it has become the largest producing sector.
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Basic Services: Government provision of hospitals, schools, police stations, courts, and defense demands expanded service infrastructure.
2. Development of Primary/Secondary Sectors: Growth in agriculture and industry drives demand for transport, storage, and trade.
3. Income Level Rise: Higher per capita income increases demand for tourism, dining out, private schooling, and shopping.
4. Information & Communication Technology: Global expansion of IT, software export, call centers, and telecommunication services.

questions.question_text:
Read the case text: 'In an urban metropolis, out of 15 lakh total workers, 11 lakh are employed in unorganized brick kilns, garment workshops, and street vending. They work 12 to 14 hours daily for meager wages without job security or healthcare.'
(i) What proportion of the urban workforce in this metropolis is in the unorganized sector? (1 mark)
(ii) State two major vulnerabilities faced by these urban casual workers. (1 mark)
(iii) Recommend two policy interventions for the municipal government to safeguard these informal workers. (2 marks)
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
(i) 11 lakh out of 15 lakh (approximately 73.3% of the workforce).
(ii) Low irregular wages, lack of job security, long unregulated hours, and zero medical safety.
(iii) Policy Interventions: 1. Strict enforcement of minimum wage regulations; 2. Issue street vendor licenses and extend subsidized state health insurance.

questions.question_text: Indian Railways and India Post are prime examples of enterprises owned by which sector?
Which economic sector contributes over 50% to India's Gross Domestic Product (GDP)?
Manufacturing bricks from clay and spinning yarn from cotton raw fiber belong to which sector?
What are Final Goods? Why are only final goods directly counted in GDP computation?
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Definition: Final goods are products consumed directly by end-users without undergoing further industrial processing.
2. Reason for Computation: The market price of final goods already includes the value of all intermediate inputs used in production. Counting intermediate goods separately leads to double counting.

questions.question_text: How can formal bank credit expansion help small farmers transition from disguised underemployment to productive farming?
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Equipment Purchase: Credit allows farmers to purchase tube-well pumpsets, high-yield seeds, and fertilizers.
2. Multi-Cropping: Irrigation enables growing second and third winter crops, keeping family members gainfully employed year-round.
3. Asset Creation: Enables investment in dairy cattle or poultry, creating secondary farm income streams.

questions.question_text: Discuss the major problems faced by unorganised sector workers in both rural and urban India. Suggest four legislative and social welfare measures to protect them.
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Problems Faced:
   - Rural: Landless agricultural laborers face seasonal unemployment, low wages, and debt bondage.
   - Urban: Casual construction/workshop workers face long hours, unsafe working conditions, low pay, and lack of housing.
2. Four Protective Measures:
   - Enforce Minimum Wages Act strictly across small workshops and agricultural farms.
   - Extend statutory pension and health insurance schemes (e.g. Ayushman Bharat/PF) to informal workers.
   - Provide low-interest institutional micro-credit to prevent debt exploitation by informal contractors.
   - Setup statutory social security boards for casual construction and head-load workers.

questions.question_text:
Read the agricultural case study: 'In a rain-fed farming village, small farmers work intensely during monsoon sowing and harvesting months (July-October), but remain completely idle during dry winter months (November-April), migrating to distant cities for casual masonry work.'
(i) Identify the specific type of employment problem occurring in dry winter months. (1 mark)
(ii) How does seasonal unemployment differ from disguised unemployment? (1 mark)
(iii) Explain how MGNREGA 2005 addresses rural seasonal unemployment. (2 marks)
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
(i) Seasonal Unemployment.
(ii) Seasonal unemployment occurs when workers find no work during specific lean months; disguised unemployment occurs when workers appear employed year-round but their marginal productivity is zero.
(iii) MGNREGA provides guaranteed 100 days of rural manual work during lean non-agricultural dry months, stemming distress urban migration.

questions.question_text: What economic situation requires two trading partners to simultaneously possess commodities desired by each other in a barter system?
options: Option B) Double Coincidence of Wants
questions.correct_answer: Option B) Double Coincidence of Wants

questions.question_text: Which institution holds the sole legal authority to issue currency notes in India on behalf of the Central Government?
options: Option A) State Bank of India
Option C) Reserve Bank of India (RBI)
questions.correct_answer: Option C) Reserve Bank of India (RBI)

questions.question_text: What approximate percentage of total deposits do commercial banks in India retain as liquid cash reserves for daily withdrawals?
How does money act as an intermediate medium of exchange to eliminate the friction of double coincidence of wants?
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Barter Friction: In barter, a shoe maker wanting wheat must find a wheat farmer who specifically wants shoes.
2. Money's Role: Money acts as a universal medium of exchange. The shoe maker sells shoes for money and uses that money to buy wheat independently, separating selling from buying.

questions.question_text: Define Collateral. State two examples of acceptable collateral assets demanded by formal commercial banks.
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Definition: Collateral is an asset owned by a borrower (land title, house, bank deposit, vehicle, livestock) pledged to a lender as security until loan clearance.
2. Examples: Land title deeds, Bank Fixed Deposit (FD) certificates, Property papers.

questions.question_text: Compare the Formal Credit Sector with the Informal Credit Sector in India across regulatory oversight, interest rates, collateral requirements, and recovery methods.
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Regulatory Oversight: Formal sector (Banks & Cooperatives) is supervised by RBI; Informal sector (Moneylenders, Landlords, Traders) operates without any regulatory body.
2. Interest Rates: Formal sector charges reasonable, regulated interest rates (8-12% p.a.); Informal sector charges exorbitant interest rates (36-60% p.a.).
3. Collateral & Documentation: Formal sector strictly requires formal collateral and income documents; Informal sector usually requires no formal collateral.
4. Recovery Methods: Formal sector uses legal procedures; Informal sector uses coercive, illegal, and physical harassment methods.

questions.question_text:
Read the credit case study: 'Salim, a shoe manufacturer, receives a festive order for 3,000 pairs of shoes. He secures raw leather on credit from suppliers and obtains a cash advance from the buyer. He completes production on time, earns profit, and repays all loans.'
(i) What role did credit play in Salim's business operation? (1 mark)
(ii) Why is Salim's case an example of a Virtuous Credit Cycle? (1 mark)
(iii) What two conditions determine whether credit will result in profit or debt? (2 marks)
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
(i) Credit provided working capital to purchase raw materials and pay labor wages.
(ii) Credit enhanced production capacity, generated net profit, and allowed prompt loan clearance, leaving Salim financially better off.
(iii) 1. Risk involved in the business enterprise; 2. Presence of crop failure or market demand uncertainty.

questions.question_text: A written paper instrument instructing a bank to pay a specific sum from a drawer's account to a payee's account is called a:
Which central body monitors commercial banks to ensure they maintain statutory cash balances and extend priority sector credit?
options: Option A) State Bank of India
Option B) Reserve Bank of India
Option D) Securities and Exchange Board of India
questions.correct_answer: Option B) Reserve Bank of India

questions.question_text: Informal moneylenders in rural villages typically charge annual interest rates in which range?
What are Demand Deposits? Mention two features that make demand deposits function as modern money.
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Definition: Bank account deposits that can be withdrawn on demand by the account holder.
2. Money Features:
   - Checkable: Cheques drawn against demand deposits settle payments directly without physical cash.
   - Universal Acceptance: Widely accepted by merchants as legal settlement alongside paper currency.

questions.question_text: Explain how commercial banks earn net income through financial intermediation (the interest rate spread).
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Intermediation: Banks collect surplus savings from depositors and lend out ~85% to borrowers.
2. Interest Gap: Banks charge higher interest rates on loans (e.g. 10-12%) and pay lower interest rates on deposits (e.g. 4%).
3. Net Spread: The difference between total loan interest collected and deposit interest paid forms bank net income.

questions.question_text: Describe the organization, operating mechanism, and socio-economic benefits of Self-Help Groups (SHGs) for rural poor women in India.
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Organization: 15 to 20 members (predominantly rural women) from a neighborhood meet and pool weekly savings (₹25 to ₹100).
2. Operating Mechanism:
   - Members take small internal micro-loans from pooled savings at reasonable interest rates.
   - After 1-2 years of regular savings and loan discipline, the SHG becomes eligible for collateral-free bank loans.
3. Benefits:
   - Overcomes collateral deficiency; peer group responsibility guarantees repayment.
   - Empowers rural women financially, fostering self-reliance and domestic decision-making power.

questions.question_text:
Read the agricultural credit case: 'Swapna, a small farmer, borrows ₹20,000 from a local moneylender at 60% annual interest to cultivate groundnut. Pests destroy her crop despite pesticide spraying. She cannot repay the loan, and compounding debt forces her to sell a portion of her land.'
(i) What type of credit situation did Swapna experience? (1 mark)
(ii) Define Debt Trap as illustrated in Swapna's case. (1 mark)
(iii) Suggest two institutional measures to prevent small farmers from falling into debt traps. (2 marks)
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
(i) A Vicious Credit Situation (Debt Trap).
(ii) Debt Trap: A condition where credit pushes a borrower into a cycle of compounding debt that forces asset or land sales to repay prior loans.
(iii) Measures: 1. Expand formal crop loans via Rural Cooperative Banks; 2. Provide state-subsidized crop insurance against pest attacks and droughts.

questions.question_text: Which Nobel Peace Laureate established the Grameen Bank of Bangladesh in the 1970s to provide collateral-free micro-credit to poor women?
Which of the following is NOT a component included under 'Terms of Credit'?
What is the primary reason why poor rural households remain dependent on informal moneylenders despite high interest rates?
options: Option A) Informal lenders provide free seeds
Option B) Lack of formal collateral and income documentation required by commercial banks
Option C) Banks charge higher interest than moneylenders
Option D) Moneylenders are owned by government
questions.correct_answer: Option B) Lack of formal collateral and income documentation required by commercial banks

questions.question_text: Explain the four main elements included under 'Terms of Credit'.
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Interest Rate: Specified percentage charged on the principal loan amount.
2. Collateral Security: Asset pledged to lender to back the loan.
3. Documentation Required: Employment proof, salary slips, or land ownership deeds.
4. Mode of Repayment: Schedule, tenure, and installment vehicle (cash/cheque) for clearing debt.

questions.question_text: Why is cheap and affordable formal credit crucial for national economic development?
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Agrarian Investments: Enables small farmers to buy high-yield seeds, fertilizers, and tube-wells without debt traps.
2. Micro-Enterprises: Allows small entrepreneurs to establish cottage industries and service units.
3. Inclusive Growth: Reduces income inequality by freeing poor households from exploitative informal moneylenders.

questions.question_text: Explain why Reserve Bank of India (RBI) supervision of commercial banks is necessary for maintaining economic stability and social equity.
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Cash Reserve Maintenance: RBI verifies that commercial banks maintain mandatory liquid cash reserves (~15%) to meet daily depositor withdrawals.
2. Equitable Credit Distribution: RBI ensures banks do not lend exclusively to profit-making big businesses, mandating credit allocation to small farmers, micro-enterprises, and weak sections.
3. Interest Rate & Liquidity Monitoring: RBI regulates interest rate structures and inspects bank financial health to protect public deposits from insolvency.

questions.question_text:
Read the housing loan case: 'Megha borrows ₹5 lakhs from a commercial bank to purchase a house at 12% annual interest for 10 years. She submits salary slips and employment records. The bank retains original house ownership papers as collateral until total loan repayment.'
(i) Identify the four terms of credit in Megha's transaction. (2 marks)
(ii) What right does the bank retain if Megha defaults on monthly installments? (1 mark)
(iii) Why is Megha's loan classified as formal sector credit? (1 mark)
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
(i) Interest Rate: 12% p.a.; Collateral: House ownership papers; Documentation: Salary slips/employment record; Repayment Mode: Monthly installments over 10 years.
(ii) The bank has the legal right to sell the collateral house property to recover unpaid loan balances.
(iii) Because it is extended by a regulated commercial bank supervised by the Reserve Bank of India.

questions.question_text: Bank account balances that can be withdrawn on demand by cash or cheque are termed:
The 9-digit code printed at the bottom of a cheque leaf used for automated electronic processing is the:
An asset owned by a borrower and pledged to a lender as security for a loan is called:
Why is modern paper currency accepted as a valid medium of exchange in India despite having no intrinsic commodity value?
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Legal Authorization: Issued exclusively by the Reserve Bank of India on behalf of the Central Government.
2. Legal Guarantee: Authorized by law as legal tender; no individual in India can legally refuse payment made in rupees.

questions.question_text: Explain how peer group responsibility in Self-Help Groups (SHGs) enables members to secure formal bank loans without individual land collateral.
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Joint Responsibility: The entire SHG is collective guarantor for loan repayment.
2. Peer Pressure: If one member defaults, other members follow up to ensure repayment, minimizing credit risk.
3. Bank Trust: Commercial banks view collective SHG savings discipline as adequate financial security, waiving individual collateral.

questions.question_text: 'Credit can play a highly positive role or a severely negative role depending on the risk and circumstances of the borrower.' Analyze this statement using the cases of Salim (shoe manufacturer) and Swapna (small farmer).
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Positive Role (Salim):
   - Credit provided working capital to fulfill festive shoe orders.
   - Enhanced business capacity, generated net profit, and allowed prompt loan repayment, improving financial standing.
2. Negative Role (Swapna):
   - Credit taken for crop production failed due to pest damage and monsoon failure.
   - High informal interest rates compounded debt, forcing land sale and pushing her into a debt trap.
3. Conclusion: Credit is beneficial when backed by stable demand and risk mitigation; it becomes hazardous in high-risk agricultural settings lacking crop insurance.

questions.question_text:
Read the excerpt: 'Grameen Bank of Bangladesh started in the 1970s as a small project by Prof. Muhammad Yunus. By 2018, it supported over 9 million poor members across 81,000 villages, 97% of whom were poor rural women who proved to be reliable micro-borrowers.'
(i) Who founded Grameen Bank of Bangladesh? (1 mark)
(ii) What percentage of Grameen Bank borrowers are rural women? (1 mark)
(iii) Explain how micro-credit empowers poor women and drives rural development. (2 marks)
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
(i) Prof. Muhammad Yunus.
(ii) 97% of total borrowers.
(iii) Micro-credit enables poor women to start small income-generating activities (poultry, weaving, retail), building self-reliance and improving household nutrition.

questions.question_text: What proportion of total deposits do commercial banks extend as credit/loans to borrowers?
Which credit sector comprises moneylenders, traders, landlords, friends, and relatives?
What is a major advantage of formal bank loans compared to informal moneylender loans?
options: Option A) Formal loans require no paperwork
Option B) Formal loans charge low, regulated interest rates
Option C) Formal loans do not need to be repaid
Option D) Formal loans are given without identification
questions.correct_answer: Option B) Formal loans charge low, regulated interest rates

questions.question_text: How do cashless money transfers using cheques reduce physical cash reliance in commercial business transactions?
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Direct Transfer: A cheque instructs a bank to transfer money directly from the buyer's account to the seller's account.
2. Security: Eliminates physical cash handling, risk of theft, and currency counting errors during high-value trade transactions.

questions.question_text: Describe two measures Reserve Bank of India (RBI) implements to prevent banks from lending exclusively to big profitable corporations.
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Priority Sector Lending (PSL): RBI mandates allocating a fixed percentage of bank credit to agriculture, small farmers, and micro-enterprises.
2. Periodic Inspection: RBI collects periodic reports on bank lending distributions, interest rates, and loan terms.

questions.question_text: Examine the rural credit structure in India. Why is it necessary to expand formal bank credit and reduce rural dependence on informal moneylenders?
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Informal Sector Exploitation: Moneylenders charge 36-60% annual interest, use unfair accounting, and seize land upon default.
2. Debt Bondage: High interest rates absorb all agricultural profits, trapping small farmers in perpetual poverty.
3. Formal Sector Deficiency: Formal banks provide only ~50% of rural credit due to collateral requirements and branch absence.
4. Expansion Necessity: Expanding formal bank branches and simplifying collateral norms guarantees cheap credit, driving rural prosperity and agricultural investment.

questions.question_text:
Read the village survey report: 'In Village Rampur, rich landowners borrow from commercial banks at 10% interest per annum against land titles. Landless agricultural laborers borrow from local village landlords at 5% interest per month (60% per annum) without collateral, performing unpaid labor upon default.'
(i) Compare the interest rates paid by rich landowners vs landless laborers. (1 mark)
(ii) Why are landless laborers forced to accept exploitative informal terms? (1 mark)
(iii) Suggest two policy solutions to integrate landless laborers into the formal credit system. (2 marks)
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
(i) Rich landowners pay 10% per annum; landless laborers pay 60% per annum (six times higher).
(ii) Landless laborers lack land collateral and formal documentation required by commercial banks.
(iii) Solutions: 1. Form and link landless labor Self-Help Groups (SHGs) to banks; 2. Issue Kisan Credit Cards (KCC) based on crop shareholding rather than land titles.

questions.question_text: A corporation that owns or controls production facilities for goods or services in more than one nation is called a:
The removal of government-imposed trade barriers, quotas, and tariffs on foreign investment is known as:
In which year did the Indian government introduce major economic liberalisation reforms opening domestic markets to foreign trade?
State two ways Multinational Corporations (MNCs) interlink production across different countries.
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Direct Acquisition: Buying established local domestic companies for immediate market presence (e.g. Cargill Foods acquiring Parakh Foods).
2. Joint Ventures: Partnering with local domestic firms to share technology and capital (e.g. Ford Motors partnering with Mahindra & Mahindra).

questions.question_text: What are Special Economic Zones (SEZs)? State two special incentives provided in SEZs.
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Definition: Dedicated industrial parks created by governments to attract Foreign Direct Investment (FDI).
2. Incentives:
   - Initial 5-year tax holiday exemption on corporate profits.
   - World-class infrastructure (electricity, water, roads) and flexible labor laws.

questions.question_text: Analyze the technological factors that have enabled globalisation, focusing on innovations in logistics containerization and Information Technology (IT).
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Containerization in Transportation:
   - Standardized sea/rail containers allow efficient multi-modal freight handling across ports and trains.
   - Reduced port unloading turnaround time dramatically and cut cargo transport costs, enabling rapid physical trade volume growth.
2. Information & Communication Technology (ICT):
   - Telecommunications, satellite links, and high-speed internet allow real-time cross-border communication.
   - Enables instantaneous service exports (e.g. software development, news typesetting, call center outsourcing) from India to Europe and the US.

questions.question_text:
Read the MNC acquisition case: 'Cargill Foods, a large American MNC, bought over Parakh Foods, an Indian edible oil company with 4 oil refineries and a vast marketing network. Cargill became the largest edible oil producer in India, packaging 5 million pouches daily.'
(i) What strategy did Cargill Foods use to expand production in India? (1 mark)
(ii) Why do MNCs prefer acquiring established domestic companies? (1 mark)
(iii) Explain two impacts of such MNC takeovers on domestic consumers and local competitors. (2 marks)
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
(i) Direct acquisition / buyout of an established local domestic company.
(ii) To gain instant control over existing distribution networks, brand reputation, and factory infrastructure.
(iii) Consumers gain access to mass-produced branded products; local competitors face displacement or market share loss.

questions.question_text: Which international body establishes rules for global free trade among member nations?
options: Option D) United Nations Development Programme

questions.question_text: Standardized metal cargo units used in sea shipping that drastically cut port handling costs are called:
A government-imposed tax on imported goods designed to protect domestic industries is a:
options: Option B) Import Tariff / Trade Barrier
questions.correct_answer: Option B) Import Tariff / Trade Barrier

questions.question_text: Explain why the Indian government placed trade barriers on foreign imports after independence (1950s-1980s), and why it removed them in 1991.
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Post-Independence (1950s-1980s): Tariffs and quotas protected infant domestic industries from foreign competition during early industrialization.
2. 1991 Reforms: Barriers were removed because the government realized domestic producers needed global competition to improve quality and efficiency.

questions.question_text: What is Foreign Direct Investment (FDI)? How does FDI differ from domestic investment?
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Definition: Capital investment made by a foreign MNC to buy land, buildings, assets, or machinery in another country.
2. Difference: Domestic investment uses local capital by native residents; FDI introduces foreign capital, advanced technology, and global production networks.

questions.question_text: 'The impact of globalisation has been uneven across different socio-economic groups in India.' Support this statement with an analysis of winners versus losers.
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Winners / Positive Impact:
   - Urban Wealthy Consumers: Access to global brands, superior quality, and low competitive prices.
   - Large Indian MNCs: Companies like Tata Motors, Infosys, and Ranbaxy expanded globally.
   - IT Service Professionals: Massive employment boom in software, call centers, and engineering.
2. Losers / Negative Impact:
   - Small Industrial Producers: Units manufacturing capacitors, batteries, and toys shut down due to cheap imports.
   - Unorganised Workers: Flexible labor laws led to insecure, casual employment without job safety.

questions.question_text:
Read the automobile case study: 'Ford Motors, an American MNC, established a major plant near Chennai investing ₹1,700 crore in partnership with Mahindra & Mahindra. The Chennai plant manufactures 1,70,000 cars annually for Indian markets and exports car components globally.'
(i) Identify the mode of production link Ford Motors used in India. (1 mark)
(ii) State two reasons why Ford Motors selected Chennai for its manufacturing hub. (1 mark)
(iii) How does establishing export component plants benefit both the MNC and the host nation? (2 marks)
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
(i) Joint Venture / Partnership with a local firm (Mahindra & Mahindra).
(ii) Availability of skilled low-cost labor and proximity to Chennai sea port for component export logistics.
(iii) MNC cuts manufacturing costs by 50-60%; Host nation gains foreign direct investment (FDI), technology transfer, and export revenue.

questions.question_text: As of recent counts, how many member countries belong to the World Trade Organisation (WTO)?
An industrial territory offering 5-year tax holidays, world-class utilities, and flexible labor laws to attract MNC investment is a:
Which Indian service sector experienced a massive export boom due to globalisation and telecommunications?
Explain the major criticism leveled against the World Trade Organisation (WTO) regarding agricultural trade policies.
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Developing Country Constraint: WTO rules force developing nations to eliminate import tariffs and trade barriers.
2. Developed Country Subsidies: Developed countries (e.g. US/EU) retain massive domestic agricultural subsidies, allowing their farmers to dump cheap produce in developing markets unfairly.

questions.question_text: How do MNCs reduce overall production costs by 50% to 60% through global location strategies?
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Research & Design: Placed in developed nations (USA/Europe) with advanced research infrastructure.
2. Low-Cost Manufacturing: Placed in countries like China with cheap labor and raw materials.
3. Technical Customer Support: Placed in English-speaking nations like India with skilled technical graduates.

questions.question_text: Examine the policy measures that government and international bodies should implement to ensure 'Fair Globalisation' that benefits all sections of society.
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Strict Labor Law Enforcement: Government must protect workers' rights and ensure job security in formal and informal sectors.
2. Support for Small Producers: Provide subsidized credit, technology, and infrastructure to small domestic units until they can compete globally.
3. Use Trade Barriers Strategically: Deploy import tariffs selectively to prevent dumping of cheap foreign goods.
4. Developing Nation Alliances: Negotiate collectively at the WTO alongside other developing countries to force developed nations to reduce agricultural subsidies.

questions.question_text:
Read the small producer case: 'Ravi started a small capacitor manufacturing unit in Hosur in 1992. After liberalisation, the government removed import duties on capacitors. Large MNCs flooded the market with cheap imported capacitors, forcing Ravi to lay off workers and close his factory.'
(i) What policy change directly impacted Ravi's capacitor unit? (1 mark)
(ii) Why was Ravi unable to compete with MNC capacitor imports? (1 mark)
(iii) What protective steps should the state take to safeguard small domestic manufacturers during trade liberalisation? (2 marks)
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
(i) Removal of import duties / trade liberalisation on electronic components.
(ii) MNCs produced capacitors at massive global scale with lower unit costs and advanced technology.
(iii) Steps: 1. Provide transition periods with phased tariff reductions; 2. Offer cheap credit and technical modernization support to domestic small units.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is an Indian multinational corporation that expanded operations globally?
The practice of placing manufacturing sub-orders with small local garment producers is known as:
What is the primary purpose of imposing import tariffs on foreign goods?
options: Option A) To increase foreign imports
Option B) To protect domestic infant industries from cheap foreign competition
Option C) To eliminate local jobs
Option D) To close domestic factories
questions.correct_answer: Option B) To protect domestic infant industries from cheap foreign competition

questions.question_text: How has containerization revolutionized international cargo logistics and ocean shipping?
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Standardized Loading: Goods are packed into huge standardized metal containers loaded directly onto ships, trains, and trucks.
2. Speed & Cost Reduction: Eliminates manual port unloading, cuts port turnaround time from days to hours, and drastically lowers freight transport costs.

questions.question_text: Explain how foreign trade leads to the integration of markets across different nations.
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Producer Expansion: Producers can sell goods beyond domestic boundaries into international markets.
2. Consumer Choice: Consumers get access to goods produced worldwide beyond domestic production.
3. Price Equalization: Prices of similar goods across distant markets tend to become equalized through competitive trade flows.

questions.question_text: Describe how Multinational Corporations (MNCs) control and spread production globally through joint ventures, buyouts, and sub-contracting networks.
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Joint Ventures: Form partnerships with local companies (e.g. Ford and Mahindra), providing capital and modern technology.
2. Domestic Buyouts: Buy out established local brands (e.g. Cargill buying Parakh Foods) to instantly acquire production plants and marketing networks.
3. Sub-contracting Networks: Place production orders for garments, footwear, and sports items with thousands of small producers worldwide, selling under MNC brand names.
4. Market Control: MNCs dictate product prices, quality standards, delivery schedules, and labor terms globally.

questions.question_text:
Read the IT service export case: 'A London news magazine publisher contracts a Delhi media firm to design and typeset its weekly magazine. The news text is transmitted via satellite to Delhi computers. Designers in Delhi compose layouts, send digital proofs back to London over the internet, and print the magazine in Delhi for air-freight back to London.'
(i) Identify the two technological enablers utilized in this service export. (1 mark)
(ii) Why did the London publisher outsource magazine design to Delhi? (1 mark)
(iii) Explain how ICT enables trade in services without physical movement of personnel. (2 marks)
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
(i) High-speed Internet and Satellite Telecommunications.
(ii) Availability of skilled English-speaking designers in India at lower operational costs.
(iii) Digital text and graphics files are transmitted instantaneously over telecommunication links, bypassing physical travel or postal shipping.

questions.question_text: Capital investment made by foreign MNCs in land, factories, and equipment in another country is called:
What term describes the policy of removing state restrictions and tariffs on foreign trade?
Which section of Indian workers was negatively impacted by globalisation due to flexible labor laws?
options: Option C) Unorganised and casual factory laborers
questions.correct_answer: Option C) Unorganised and casual factory laborers

questions.question_text: How have urban middle-class consumers in India benefited from the process of globalisation?
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Product Variety: Access to a wide array of global brands in electronics, automobiles, and clothing.
2. Improved Quality: Foreign competition improved product quality and introduced modern technology.
3. Lower Prices: Intense market competition reduced prices for consumer goods like smartphones and televisions.

questions.question_text: Why do foreign MNCs set up customer support call centers and IT hubs in India?
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Skilled Workforce: Large pool of educated, English-speaking engineering and technical graduates.
2. Cost Savings: Indian wages and office operational costs are substantially lower than in North America or Europe.
3. Time-Zone Advantage: Allows 24/7 continuous business processing for Western clients.

questions.question_text: Analyze the dual impact of the 1991 economic reforms on Indian domestic manufacturing industries and employment security.
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Impact on Manufacturing Industries:
   - Large corporations (Tata, Ranbaxy, Mahindra) modernized, adopted advanced technology, and became global MNCs.
   - Small domestic producers (batteries, capacitors, plastic toys) were crushed by cheap mass-produced foreign imports, leading to widespread factory closures.
2. Impact on Employment Security:
   - To compete globally, Indian manufacturers demanded 'flexible labor laws', hiring workers casually during peak seasons and firing them without severance during lean periods.
   - Workers lost job security, statutory provident fund, and healthcare cover, forcing millions into vulnerable unorganized employment.

questions.question_text:
Read the garment factory case: 'Garment export units in urban industrial parks hire female workers on temporary contracts during peak European winter fashion orders. Workers work 10 to 12 hours daily, including mandatory unpaid overtime. When orders drop, workers are dismissed immediately without notice.'
(i) What labor practice is illustrated in this garment export unit? (1 mark)
(ii) Why do garment MNCs pressure Indian factory owners for flexible hiring terms? (1 mark)
(iii) Suggest two statutory reforms to protect casual garment workers while maintaining export competitiveness. (2 marks)
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
(i) Flexible / Temporary casual labor practices.
(ii) To minimize labor costs during lean seasons and maximize export profit margins.
(iii) Statutory Reforms: 1. Enforce mandatory overtime wage rates; 2. Require employers to contribute to statutory unemployment insurance funds.

questions.question_text: National Consumers Day is celebrated in India every year on which date to mark presidential assent to COPRA in 1986?
Which statutory act passed in 1986 created the three-tier quasi-judicial consumer disputes redressal system in India?
What official quality certification logo is marked on agricultural produce such as honey, pulses, and edible oils in India?
Explain the historical origin of the consumer movement in India during the 1960s.
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Social Discontent: Emerged in response to rampant market exploitation including food shortages, hoarding, black marketing, and adulteration of food grains.
2. Grassroots Activism: Consumer groups published articles, held exhibitions, and pressured the government to regulate unfair trade practices.
3. Legislative Outcome: Sustained pressure forced the Indian Parliament to enact COPRA in December 1986.

questions.question_text: What is the 'Right to Safety'? Give a real-world medical negligence example.
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Definition: Entitles consumers to protection against goods and services that are hazardous to life, health, or bodily safety.
2. Example: Reji Mathew, a Class IX student paralyzed due to defective anesthesia during tonsillectomy surgery, whose family received compensation under Right to Safety.

questions.question_text: Describe the three-tier quasi-judicial consumer disputes redressal structure established under COPRA 2019 rules, including claim financial limits and appeal channels.
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission: Handles original claims up to ₹1 Crore.
2. State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission: Handles original claims between ₹1 Crore and ₹10 Crore, plus appeals against District Commission orders.
3. National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (New Delhi): Handles original claims exceeding ₹10 Crore, plus appeals against State Commission orders.
4. Supreme Court Appeal: Any party aggrieved by the National Commission order can appeal to the Supreme Court of India.

questions.question_text:
Read the hospital negligence case study: 'Reji Mathew underwent tonsillectomy at a private clinic. Improper anesthesia administration by the surgeon caused severe brain injury, leaving Reji paralyzed. Reji's father filed a complaint seeking compensation for medical negligence.'
(i) Which statutory consumer right was violated in Reji's case? (1 mark)
(ii) In which consumer commissions did Reji's father file his compensation claim? (1 mark)
(iii) What final relief did the Consumer Forum award to Reji's family? (2 marks)
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
(i) Right to Safety.
(ii) State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission and National Consumer Commission.
(iii) The National Commission held the clinic guilty of medical negligence and awarded ₹5 lakh statutory compensation to Reji's family.

questions.question_text: Which standardisation mark is mandatory on electrical appliances such as pressure cookers and LPG cylinders in India?
Under 2019 COPRA rules, a consumer dispute claim worth ₹45 lakhs must be directly filed in which commission?
Which statutory act passed in 2005 empowers Indian citizens to demand official records regarding government operations?
options: Option B) Right to Information (RTI) Act 2005
questions.correct_answer: Option B) Right to Information (RTI) Act 2005

questions.question_text: Explain how the 'Right to Information' (RTI) protects consumers when purchasing packaged commodities.
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Mandatory Label Details: Package must disclose ingredients, net weight, Maximum Retail Price (MRP), batch number, manufacturing date, and expiry date.
2. Seller Accountability: Enables buyers to reject expired products, verify ingredient safety, and challenge sales above printed MRP.

questions.question_text: Why is obtaining a formal cash receipt/bill essential when purchasing goods or services?
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Documentary Evidence: Serves as legal proof of transaction required by Consumer Commissions.
2. Legal Enforceability: Without a bill, shopkeepers can deny selling the product, making dispute compensation impossible.

questions.question_text: Examine the six statutory consumer rights granted under COPRA. Explain any four rights with appropriate real-world market examples.
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Right to Safety: Protection against life-threatening products (e.g. defective electrical irons, medical negligence).
2. Right to Information: Mandates disclosure of product details (MRP, batch number, expiry date).
3. Right to Choose: Freedom to select products without forced conditional bundling (e.g. refusal to sell toothpaste unless toothbrush is bought).
4. Right to Seek Redressal: Right to fair compensation, repair, or replacement for defective items.
5. Right to Representation: Filing claims in consumer courts.
6. Right to Consumer Education: Promoting consumer literacy.

questions.question_text:
Read the retail dispute case: 'Abirami bought a defective wall clock from a local dealer. When she requested a replacement, the dealer refused because she lost her cash receipt. She engaged an advocate and filed a complaint in the District Consumer Commission using her stamped warranty card.'
(i) Why did the dealer refuse initial product replacement? (1 mark)
(ii) In which consumer forum did Abirami file her complaint? (1 mark)
(iii) Why should consumers demand bills and retain warranty cards for major purchases? (2 marks)
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
(i) Because Abirami could not produce the formal cash receipt as proof of purchase.
(ii) District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission.
(iii) Cash bills and warranty cards provide legal documentary evidence establishing seller liability before consumer courts.

questions.question_text: Which standardisation mark is used in India to certify the purity of gold and silver jewelry?
Under 2019 COPRA rules, original consumer claim values ranging between ₹1 Crore and ₹10 Crore fall under which jurisdiction?
What legal doctrine meaning 'let the buyer beware' was historically exploited by unorganized shopkeepers?
Explain the 'Right to Choose' with an example of illegal product bundling.
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Definition: Any consumer receiving a good or service has the freedom to choose what to buy without conditional pressure.
2. Example: A shopkeeper refusing to sell a gas connection unless the buyer purchases a specific brand of gas stove from the same shop.

questions.question_text: What is Maximum Retail Price (MRP)? Why is selling a packaged product above printed MRP illegal?
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Definition: MRP is the maximum legal retail price printed on a package, inclusive of all local and central taxes.
2. Illegal Status: Charging above printed MRP constitutes an unfair trade practice under COPRA, exploiting consumer vulnerability.

questions.question_text: Discuss the major progress achieved and ongoing implementation challenges faced by the consumer movement in India.
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Major Progress:
   - Enactment and 2019 expansion of COPRA.
   - Creation of three-tier quasi-judicial consumer courts.
   - Growing public awareness of standardisation marks (ISI, Agmark, Hallmark).
2. Ongoing Challenges:
   - Redressal proceedings are often lengthy, expensive, and delayed.
   - Informal shopkeepers rarely issue cash receipts, leaving buyers without legal evidence.
   - Consumer protection laws remain weakly enforced in small rural markets.

questions.question_text:
Read the product label scenario: 'A consumer purchases a jar of pure honey bearing the Agmark seal and a packet of digestive biscuits displaying an FSSAI logo and a green dot.'
(i) What quality attribute does the Agmark seal certify for honey? (1 mark)
(ii) What does the green dot inside a square signify on packaged food? (1 mark)
(iii) Why are government quality certification marks essential for consumer safety? (2 marks)
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
(i) Purity and quality standards of agricultural food produce.
(ii) That the packaged food product contains purely vegetarian ingredients.
(iii) Certifies that products meet statutory safety standards, protecting consumers against adulteration and electrical/chemical hazards.

questions.question_text: The apex consumer court in India located in New Delhi handling original claims exceeding ₹10 Crore is the:
options: Option B) National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission
questions.correct_answer: Option B) National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission

questions.question_text: Which national government agency issues ISI and Hallmark quality certification marks in India?
options: Option A) Food Corporation of India
Option B) Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS)
questions.correct_answer: Option B) Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS)

questions.question_text: Which consumer right guarantees that aggrieved buyers can present their grievances in consumer forums?
options: Option B) Right to be Heard / Representation
questions.correct_answer: Option B) Right to be Heard / Representation

questions.question_text: Distinguish between Consumer Protection Councils and Consumer Disputes Redressal Commissions.
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
Consumer Protection Councils: Advisory bodies at district, state, and national levels promoting consumer awareness and education.
Consumer Disputes Redressal Commissions: Quasi-judicial courts holding legal authority to adjudicate dispute claims, enforce compensation, and punish unfair trade practices.

questions.question_text: How does consumer awareness protect buyers against common market exploitation like under-weighing and adulteration?
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Verification: Informed consumers inspect weights, check batch numbers, and insist on certified logos (ISI, Agmark).
2. Assertiveness: Aware buyers insist on cash bills and report unfair trade practices to consumer forums, deterring shopkeeper fraud.

questions.question_text: 'Unorganized market sellers exploit consumers through various unfair trade practices.' Evaluate this statement with five common forms of consumer exploitation.
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Adulteration: Mixing substandard or harmful substances into food grains, milk, and edible oils.
2. Under-weighing / Under-measuring: Modifying electronic scales or measuring tapes to deliver less quantity.
3. False Advertising: Making deceptive claims regarding product quality, durability, or health benefits.
4. Overcharging above MRP: Selling essential goods above printed Maximum Retail Price during artificial scarcity.
5. Defective / Hazardous Goods: Selling uncertified electrical appliances that pose fire or electrocution risks.

questions.question_text:
Read the conditional sale case: 'A retail shopkeeper refuses to sell a bottle of toothpaste to a customer unless the customer also purchases a toothbrush from his shop.'
(i) Which statutory consumer right was violated by the shopkeeper? (1 mark)
(ii) Why is conditional bundling of products illegal under COPRA? (1 mark)
(iii) What action can the customer take against the shopkeeper? (2 marks)
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
(i) Right to Choose.
(ii) Because it forces consumers to spend money on unwanted items as a condition for buying essential goods.
(iii) Action: 1. Demand to buy the toothpaste independently; 2. File a formal complaint before the District Consumer Commission for unfair trade practice.

questions.question_text: Which autonomous regulatory authority regulates food safety standards and issues food packaging logos in India?
What is the final judicial court of appeal above the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission?
options: Option B) Supreme Court of India
Option C) International Court of Justice
questions.correct_answer: Option B) Supreme Court of India

questions.question_text: A green dot symbol printed on packaged food items in India signifies that the product is:
Explain the 'Right to Seek Redressal'. State two types of relief consumer courts can award to victims.
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Definition: Guarantees consumers the right to seek fair compensation, replacement, or repair for defective goods or deficient services.
2. Reliefs Awarded:
   - Order replacement of defective product or full monetary refund.
   - Award financial compensation for physical injury, loss, or mental harassment.

questions.question_text: Why is December 24 observed as National Consumers Day in India?
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Presidential Assent: On December 24, 1986, the Consumer Protection Act (COPRA) received official presidential assent.
2. Milestone: Enactment marked the statutory birth of consumer rights and quasi-judicial protection in India.

questions.question_text: Analyze how quality standardisation logos (ISI, Agmark, Hallmark) protect consumers from substandard products. Explain the regulatory role of the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS).
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
1. Role of Quality Logos:
   - ISI Mark: Ensures electrical appliances, pressure cookers, and LPG cylinders meet strict safety norms, preventing accidents.
   - Agmark: Certifies agricultural food produce purity, preventing health hazards from adulteration.
   - Hallmark: Guarantees official fineness and purity of gold jewelry.
2. Role of Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS):
   - Sets scientific quality benchmarks, inspects manufacturing facilities, and grants certification licenses to manufacturers complying with safety standards.

questions.question_text:
Read the RTI case study: 'A resident of Municipal Ward 4 filed an application under the Right to Information (RTI Act 2005) demanding official records regarding a 2-year delay in completing a local drinking water pipeline project.'
(i) Which statutory act enabled the resident to demand government project records? (1 mark)
(ii) How does RTI promote administrative transparency and accountability? (1 mark)
(iii) Explain how citizens can use RTI to challenge corruption and public service deficiencies. (2 marks)
questions.marking_scheme_answer:
(i) Right to Information (RTI) Act 2005.
(ii) By granting citizens legal access to official government documents, tender files, and project execution records.
(iii) Citizens inspect public works, uncover administrative delays or financial misuse, and hold public officials accountable under law.

case_study_viewport.case_title: Case Study Viewport: Salim vs Swapna Credit Outcomes
case_study_viewport.scenario_text: Salim receives a festive order for 3,000 pairs of shoes. He borrows working capital credit, completes delivery, earns profit, and repays the bank. Swapna borrows money from a local moneylender for groundnut farming. Pests ruin her crop, causing severe debt that forces her to sell part of her land.
